header.title: Fierabras (V): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:transcr-fier-v:norm, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.1: Line 1: unc is unclear; read as un, '[a piece]' of the coif. Line 13: chaval read as cheval 'horse'; a horse is odd in this exchange of blows, and the word may be corrupt. Line 30: li signe aouré, 'the worshipped sign', apparently another Passion relic (the nails?). Line 35: mer read as muir, 'I die'.
notes.87: Line 104: O le read as o la, 'with her'. Line 110: pevree, a pepper sauce, a stock image of blackness. Line 118: o le chief de l espee taken as 'on the head with the sword'; it could be 'with the tip of the sword'. Line 122: terre sauvee, 'saved land', perhaps Christendom; sense unsure.
notes.69: Line 70: a peeled apple, a stock image of something worthless. Line 71: d aigre moree taken as the place name Aigremoree. Line 72: mer betee, the 'curdled' (frozen) sea of the far north, a stock phrase. Line 74: flori. is abbreviated Floripas. Line 80: aincois ... que may instead mean 'before the dew appears'.

nodes.text: He knocked [a piece] of the coif at the skull down onto the meadow
and shaved off a great part of the hair of his head;
the Lord God protected him, so that he did not touch him in the flesh.
And the count strikes him back with fierce strength;
he aimed a great blow at him on the jewelled helmet.
Fierabras sees the blow that he has aimed at him;
what he held of the shield he has thrown up against it,
so that he has left his flank and his side all uncovered.
Oliver notices it, he has marked it very well;
on the backstroke he strikes him with the inscribed blade;
he has given him a great blow above the breast.
He has torn and broken the mail of his white hauberk;
the horse beneath him he has cut all to pieces.
The count pressed on him, for his heart was angry;
he has put all his strength into it, and thrust his blade well in.
Along the left flank he has slid the blade into him;
right into the middle of the back he has slashed and cut him;
his bowels very nearly flew out.
But none of them was harmed or damaged there.
The blood pours out of his side in great abundance.
Hear of Fierabras, how great his pride was.
Up toward the sky the king has looked;
he remembers the Lord God and the Trinity,
and his body is kindled by the Holy Spirit.
He called to Oliver, he has cried to him for mercy:
“Noble man of good birth, do not kill me, for God's sake!
And I will go to Charlemagne, the mighty crowned king,
and I promise you truly, upon my good faith,
that I will hold the faith and Christianity,
and I will give back the crown and the worshipped sign
and the holy relics, of which there are so many there.
Why did I ever take them, wretched, ill-fated man?
Shame has come to me from it, I know it truly.
Oliver, noble man, have pity on me!
If I die a Saracen, it will be held against you.
Baron, if you do not hold me up, you will soon see me fall here.”
The Saracens attack them, the vile, mad people,
but they never did them harm there worth a peeled apple.
The emir calls Malpin of Aigremoree;
there was no such master thief as far as the curdled sea.
“Malpin,” said the emir, “by my grizzled beard,
if you had stolen her girdle from Floripas,
the French could never again hold out against us at all.
And if you steal it for me, it is proven truth,
I will give you a great packhorse-load of my gold.
As long as they have the girdle, the tower will not be starved.”
“Sire,” said the thief, “tomorrow before evening,
or rather tomorrow at dawn, when the dew appears,
I will have handed over to you the lady's girdle.”
When the emir hears it, he has made great joy.
The day goes into decline and evening comes on.
than a squirrel [climbs] an oak in the leafy forest.
He went into the tower quietly, in secret;
swiftly and quickly he came to the hearth;
he has taken a candle and lit it at the fire;
he came to the door of the chamber and found it locked,
and he has spoken his charm: at once it is unlocked.
He sees our French sleeping in the paved hall;
the thief has beguiled and enchanted our people
so that they would not wake for the tower full of gold.
Count Gui of Burgundy, of the bold face,
was at a window facing the salt sea,
to see the great army that was gathered there.
And the thief made no longer delay;
he comes to the bed of Floripas, who was fairer than a fairy.
He searched for the girdle until he had found it;
he fastens it around himself by the golden buckle.
He looked at Floripas, who was fairer than a fairy;
he will want to lie with her, for she pleases him greatly.
He seized her by the sides and dragged her out all naked.
The maiden wakes, she has cried out aloud:
“Holy Mary, lady, crowned queen!
Where are you?” she says. “You are staying away too long.”
Her maidens run up, each with her hair loose;
when they see the thief, blacker than pepper sauce,
the boldest of them all has turned to flight.
The thief has thrown Floripas on her back beneath him;
to my knowledge, he would soon have dishonoured her.
When Gui of Burgundy heard the noise,
he comes running to the chamber at full speed;
he cries to his beloved: “Hush, fair lady!”
When the thief hears him, he leaps from the bed in a bound,
and the duke struck him with the end of the sword;
he splits him into two halves; the girdle is cut.
The thief's candle is then put out;
the enchantment lasted no longer in there.
Then the counts of the saved land leap up,
and Gui has told them the matter from beginning to end.
